response.translation: For in all the passages quoted he evidently mentions [645] both sleeplessness and coma. And again, writing of another patient in the same book, he says: 'In this man throughout, from the time that I too knew him, the bowel was disturbed, urine thin, black; he was comatose, sleepless.' So it is plainly evident that with him the name of coma signifies neither sleep nor torpor (kataphora). For this reason, I suppose, some of the exegetes say that the comatose are named from 'revelling' (kōmazein). For revellers are awake, and the comatose are awake too. And, by Zeus, just as revellers do not nod down at all, so neither do those in a coma, and especially not with their eyes. For their eyes are moist and red and unsteady and sunken. But in both the whole body is unsteady in its movements and lacking in control. For this reason, they say, Hippocrates himself is also at a loss about the whole syndrome, whether one should call these patients phrenitics or something else.

raw_text: {"translation": "'Swellings beside the ears occurred in many, on one side, and in most on both sides, in persons who were without fever and up and about; in some there was also [652] slight heating. In all they subsided without harm, and in none did they suppurate, as those that arise from other causes do.' For it is truly contrary to expectation that none suppurated, and not at all customary. Then he adds: 'Their character was lax, large, diffuse, not with inflammation'; for it is contrary to expectation that in all of them the abscessions about the ears should occur without inflammation. So here too he plainly applies the term coma to the somnolent kataphora, when he says: 'The coma was continuous, not somnolent.' He remarks on this as if it ought to be somnolent and always became so, and now, contrary to expectation, did not.
